topic_title: Understand the characteristics of basic univariate distributions and how to generate samples from them
cmp_edition: IFoA CS1 Core Reading / CMP · 2026 syllabus alignment

mission.display_title: Name the discrete distribution family by situation
mission.mission_purpose: Today's Mission exists to open the distributional spine lawfully — so you can recognise basic discrete univariate distributions by the situations they model, not by formula memorisation alone.
mission.tutor_intent: Today I will force the candidate to match counting situations to geometric, binomial, negative binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, and discrete uniform families — and to refuse treating every count as Poisson by habit.
mission.educational_intent: Produce a cognitive move from 'distributions are formula lists' to 'I can name which discrete family fits a counting / selection situation and why.'
mission.learning_objective: Describe the characteristics of geometric, binomial, negative binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, and uniform discrete distributions on a finite set, and match each to a recognisable data-generating situation.
mission.concept_focus: Counting / selection situation → discrete family name → one defining characteristic (support / parameter story).
mission.prior_bridge: Yesterday you closed PCA (1.2.3) as exploratory reduction with honest limits. Today those explored variables meet modelling vocabulary: Chapter 2 opens at 2.1.1 with discrete univariate distributions.
mission.why_now: 2.1.1 is the lawful first LO of the distributional chapter-family after Alpha's handoff and Beta's PCA closure; examiners expect situation-to-family recognition before deep probability calculation (2.1.3).
mission.expected_benefit: A situation→family map for the syllabus discrete set — Study Progress for today's Session, not mastery of all probability evaluations.
mission.explainability: Assigned as Campaign Beta Day 2 because Volume CS1-002's educational transformation requires lawful entry to 2.1 after PCA placement.
success_criteria: Closed-book, name the six syllabus discrete families in LO 2.1.1.
For three distinct counting/selection situations, choose the matching family and give one characteristic warrant.
Refuse one habitual mis-match (e.g. Poisson for sampling without replacement).
task_descriptions: Sketch a six-box discrete family map with one situation cue each before opening the CMP.
Complete Guided Reading through CMP treatment of Syllabus 2.1.1 discrete distributions.
Closed-book: match situations to families and refuse one mis-match.

reading_guidance.lead_line: Extract the defining situation and one characteristic for each discrete family in 2.1.1 — then stop before continuous distributions 2.1.2.
focus_questions: What counting or selection story does each of geometric, binomial, negative binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, and discrete uniform tell?
Which families involve replacement / independent trials versus without-replacement sampling?
When is Poisson a natural count model, and when is it a lazy default?
You will later match situations to families and refuse one mis-match.
misconception_watch: Watch for treating binomial and hypergeometric as interchangeable.
Watch for calling every rare-event count Poisson without rate/independence warrant.
Watch for drifting into continuous families or quantile calculation before finishing 2.1.1.

knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: discrete family roster
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Name the six discrete distribution families in Syllabus 2.1.1. For each, give one short situation cue (not a full formula).
knowledge_checks.body: Roster + situation cues; no deep probability calculation required.
hints: Geometric; binomial; negative binomial; hypergeometric; Poisson; discrete uniform.
Cues: trials-to-first-success; fixed trials successes; successes-to-r; without replacement; rare counts / rate; equally likely finite set.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Chapter 2 entry requires the family roster to retrieve before calculation theatre.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Geometric (trials to first success); binomial (successes in fixed trials); negative binomial (trials to r successes); hypergeometric (successes in without-replacement sample); Poisson (counts with rate story); discrete uniform (equally likely finite outcomes).
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Omitting hypergeometric or collapsing negative binomial into geometric.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: match and refuse mis-match
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. (1) From a finite portfolio of policies, you draw a sample without replacement and count how many are currently in claim. Which discrete family fits, and why? (2) Name one family that would be a habitual mis-match here, and refuse it in one sentence.
knowledge_checks.body: Without-replacement sampling → hypergeometric; refuse binomial/Poisson-by-habit when dependence from depletion matters.
hints: Without replacement from a finite population → hypergeometric.
Refuse: binomial (assumes independent trials / replacement) or Poisson without rate/independence warrant.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Situation discipline prevents treating every count as binomial or Poisson.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Hypergeometric — successes counted in a without-replacement sample from a finite population. Refuse binomial here if trials are not independent with constant success probability (depletion matters), or refuse Poisson-by-habit without a rate process warrant.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Default binomial or Poisson without noticing without-replacement structure.
